title: Dogs Can Read Human Emotions, Study Finds
paragraphs: Dog owners often feel that their pets can sense when they are happy or sad. Now, a new study suggests that dogs' brains really can tell the difference between some human emotions.

The study was carried out by researchers led by Raúl Hernández-Pérez and Laura Cuaya of the University of Vienna in Austria, together with scientists in Mexico and Hungary. It was published in the journal iScience in August 2026.

The researchers used a method called fMRI, which measures activity in the brain, while trained pet dogs stayed awake and looked at photos of human faces. In the first experiment, eight dogs looked at pictures of strangers with happy or neutral faces. In the second experiment, 12 dogs looked at faces that were happy, angry, fearful or sad. The researchers then used machine learning to analyze patterns of activity in the dogs' brains.

The results showed that happy faces increased activity in two parts of the dogs' brains. One is linked to higher-level thinking, and the other is linked to reward. Because of this, it was relatively easy to tell the dogs' responses to happy faces apart from their responses to negative emotions. In addition, the dogs' brains reacted differently to fearful faces than to angry or sad ones. According to the researchers, this is the first evidence that dogs can tell the difference between specific negative human expressions. However, they could not clearly distinguish anger from sadness.
Hernández-Pérez explained that, like humans, dogs are very good at noticing small details on the face. Cuaya said she would like people to see dogs as emotional beings.

However, the study had some limitations. Only a small number of dogs took part, and all of them were pets living with families. In addition, they only looked at still photos, while in real life, dogs also use body language, voices and smells to understand people. The study also does not show that dogs experience emotions in the same way as humans.
The researchers now plan to study how dogs combine different signals to understand people.
